reviewIndex.registryName: Human Geography and Planning / Sociale Geografie en Planologie

audience.programmeDescription: Human Geography and Planning at the University of Amsterdam examines how people, institutions and environments shape places. This example follows Planning, with Building the City and its separate Planning and Real Estate seminar in year two, and Moving in the City in year three.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR can emphasise people and spatial sustainability, public governance and inequality, or global connections, identity and place. These options combine relevant social, environmental and research subjects. UvA offers more sustained geographical theory, urban and property planning, mobility and supervised field research. The relationships shown are partial.

componentNotes.y2-01: This 12-credit thematic choice examines property-led urban development, land and property markets, regulation and governance. It requires a positive study recommendation or a completed first year.
componentNotes.y2-02: This separate six-credit seminar examines planning and real-estate actors, negotiation, redevelopment feasibility and residual land value. It is not a six-credit version of Building the City. A positive first-year study recommendation is required.
componentNotes.y1-06: Participate in Thinking Spatially before Research Methods 1. The methods sequence combines qualitative and quantitative social research with GIS.
componentNotes.y2-03: Pass Research Methods 1 before Research Methods 2. The latter develops GIS, thematic qualitative analysis and multivariable quantitative analysis.
componentNotes.y2-04: Pass Academic Skills and the Regional Research Project, and meet the participation requirements in Research Methods 2, before this project. A one- to two-week foreign field visit follows preparation in Amsterdam. Destination and theme are selected from the offered projects.
componentNotes.y2-05: Pass Academic Skills and meet the Research Methods 2 participation requirements. This four-week project includes a full-time residential fieldwork week in the Netherlands, then quantitative survey analysis and thematic analysis of interviews.
componentNotes.y2-06: The selected Planning specialisation requires this twelve-credit course in the theories and practices of spatial intervention.
componentNotes.y2-07: The Planning specialisation also requires this six-credit course on professional planning roles, stakeholder and site analysis and alternative policy actions. Earlier planning theory supplies its preparation.
componentNotes.y3-01: The retained twelve-credit thematic choice studies mobility and spatial development. A positive study recommendation or completed first year is required.
componentNotes.y3-02: Pass Research Methods 2 and the Netherlands Research Project before Research Methods 3. This course develops the research design and proposal and is normally taken alongside the thesis.
componentNotes.y3-03: Thirty credits remain open for university bachelor courses, a minor, an approved exchange or an approved internship. Study must take place while enrolled in the degree; vocational higher-education courses do not count. Other arrangements require Examination Board approval.
componentNotes.y3-04: The twelve-credit thesis is an individual original research project in human geography or planning, supervised within a thematic project group. Pass all first-year courses, Research Methods 2 and the Netherlands Research Project, and meet the participation requirement in Research Methods 3. The latter may run alongside the thesis.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

BENECON111.name: Introduction to Economics
BENECON111.text: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.

BENECON211.name: International Macroeconomics
BENECON211.text: Study the economy as a whole through topics such as national income, economic growth, inflation, and unemployment. Understand how governments and central banks use fiscal and monetary policies to influence economic performance over time. The course also explores business cycles, international trade, and economic crises, preparing students to evaluate policy debates and global economic trends.

BENECON311.name: Public Economics
BENECON311.text: Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.

BENECON312.name: Econometrics
BENECON312.text: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.

BENGATE102.name: Research Methods & Statistics
BENGATE102.text: Research Methods & Statistics introduces research design, operationalisation, measurement, sampling, surveys and experiments. Students study descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression using R and R Commander. A group project develops a research plan and instruments, collects and analyses data, and reports findings under research-ethics and privacy requirements.

BENLEAD211.name: Psychology of Leading Under Pressure
BENLEAD211.text: Examines how emotion regulation, emotional intelligence, belonging, identity safety and psychological safety shape leadership in diverse contexts, with particular attention to minority experiences. Students design and pilot a quantitative survey, collect data ethically, and use SPSS or RStudio for descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, correlations, group comparisons and introductory multiple regression. They interpret the findings and develop evidence-based leadership recommendations.

DISDATA111.name: Introduction to Data Science
DISDATA111.text: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.

ENSDELT211.name: Living with Water
ENSDELT211.text: Studies water risks and opportunities in deltas, using Zeeland as a central case. Flooding, freshwater scarcity, salinisation, subsidence and pollution are connected to infrastructure, history, governance, law and justice. Students evaluate engineered and nature-based responses, then apply these ideas through site-based inquiry and a project on delta adaptation.

ENSDELT312.name: Governance of Sustainability
ENSDELT312.text: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.

ENSENVI211.name: Earth Observation
ENSENVI211.text: Provides hands‑on experience with GIS and data integration using geospatial data from satellites and drones. Uncovers how human actions impact ecosystems and climate and promotes sustainable practices through research projects.

ENSENVI213.name: Earth System Science Tools
ENSENVI213.text: Explores interactions among biosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and atmosphere. Teaches system modelling, uses proxies and isotope tracers to study past and future climates and includes a field trip focused on greenhouse gas pathways.

ENSGATE101.name: Sustainability Essentials I
ENSGATE101.text: Introduces sustainability through planetary boundaries and scientific tools for understanding human impacts on Earth systems. Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and study chemical and physical principles relevant to climate, energy and materials. A laboratory project makes and tests starch-based biopolymers.

ENSSUST111.name: Climate Change
ENSSUST111.text: Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.

ENSSUST313.name: Research in a Sustainable Delta
ENSSUST313.text: In this project course you will work in small teams of two or three students on a research problem relevant for sustainability in the broadest sense. We are looking for collaborations with local companies and other institutions. The research questions are supplied by a regional institution or company that is active in areas related to sustainability in the broadest sense. In this way it is guaranteed that the research projects are indeed relevant for the Zeeland delta. Furthermore, students will have access to expertise and/or facilities of the external partner, which will broaden their perspective. Usually, there will be one person affiliated with the external partner organization involved with a project team as external advisor

GOSGATE102.name: Law, Society & Justice
GOSGATE102.text: Law, Society & Justice examines legal, social and normative perspectives on law. Students compare legal traditions and study public and private law, human rights, justice, social control and change, race and gender. Case briefs, demand letters and mock trials develop legal reasoning, while a family-law topic supports the design of a socio-legal research proposal.

GOSHIST211.text: History of Empires examines empires across global history and competing theories of empire. Students study expansion, administration, military and economic systems, legitimacy, ideology, culture, decline and legacies. Historical cases, source analysis and an independent research essay connect theoretical interpretation with specific imperial experiences.

GOSHIST311.name: Native American Histories
GOSHIST311.text: Native American Histories studies Indigenous social and cultural histories from the nineteenth century to the present. Boarding schools, institutional violence, family separation and intergenerational trauma are connected to resistance, resurgence, food sovereignty and cultural expression. Storytelling, reciprocity and relational accountability guide collaboration with Indigenous peers and knowledge holders through arts-based work and a public-history project.

GOSHIST312.text: Guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from formulating research questions to engaging critically with sources. Emphasises methodological rigour and interdisciplinary thinking and culminates in a substantial research paper.

GOSLAWJ111.text: Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.

GOSLAWJ212.name: Introduction to Public International Law
GOSLAWJ212.text: Introduction to Public International Law examines its sources, theories, institutions and relationship to domestic law. Topics include responsibility, force, armed conflict, international crime, human rights, economic relations and environmental protection, followed by self-determination, Third World approaches, compliance and treaty politics. Case exercises and a research podcast develop legal reasoning and critical analysis.

GOSLAWJ213.text: Comparative Constitutional Law compares constitutional structures, institutions and rights across legal systems and introduces administrative law. Students study federalism, legislatures, executive relationships, courts, judicial review, human rights, public participation and procedural fairness. A staged booklet compares two constitutions, supported by legal interpretation, case-law analysis and hypothetical cases.

GOSLAWJ311.text: Examines principles of property, tort and contract law and other selected areas of private law. It compares legal systems including Germany, France, England, China and the United States, and considers the social, economic and political pressures underlying legal principles.

GOSPOLI112.text: Provides analytical tools to compare political systems and democracies. Examines phenomena like democratic backsliding, decline of political parties, rise of populism, media changes, non‑majoritarian institutions and globalization’s impact on domestic politics.

Students plan the research, code amendments, assess salience and trace legislative processes.

MCCHEAM212.name: Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean
MCCHEAM212.text: This course examines the painting, sculpture, and architecture of Renaissance Italy and the extensive artistic connections that linked the Italian peninsula to other regions of the world. By exploring a range of geographical contexts, from the Islamic courts of the Eastern Mediterranean and the commercial routes connecting Europe, Asia, and Africa to the newly encountered territories of the Americas, students will examine how trade, colonization, and cross-cultural exchange shaped the production and meaning of Renaissance art.

MCCMEDI311.name: Media & Race
MCCMEDI311.text: Media & Race investigates storytelling, power, privilege, resistance and systemic racism in American history from the late nineteenth century to the present. Film, photographs, music and other media connect past and present. Students produce research-based podcasts exploring how media sustains oppression and supports resistance.
